name: Zhou Dynasty
capital: Fenghao (1046–771 BCE); Wangcheng / Chengzhou near Luoyang (771–256 BCE)
summary: The longest-lasting Chinese dynasty. It introduced the Mandate of Heaven; its later centuries (Spring and Autumn, Warring States) produced Confucius and other great thinkers.

knownFor.label: Mandate of Heaven
knownFor.note: The idea that Heaven grants and withdraws the right to rule.

knownFor.label: Confucius
knownFor.note: His teachings shaped East Asian ethics and government.

knownFor.label: The crossbow
knownFor.note: Mass-produced trigger crossbows in the Warring States.

knownFor.label: Cast iron
knownFor.note: Chinese smiths cast iron centuries before Europe.

location.value: First the Wei River valley (Western Zhou), then the Luoyang area after 771 BCE (Eastern Zhou). Its client states spread across the North China Plain and later the Yangtze region.

terrain.value: The Wei River valley, the loess plateau, the Yellow River and the North China Plain. Mountain passes protected the western homeland.

climate.value: Seasonal monsoon climate. Natural calamities and eclipses were read as omens that Heaven might withdraw its mandate.

resources.value: Millet and wheat farmland, and bronze (later iron) for weapons and tools. Large irrigation works were built in the Warring States period.

disasters.value: Earthquakes, eclipses and droughts are recorded as omens, but specific disasters are not well documented.

population.value: Wikipedia’s infobox gives about 30 million people in 273 BCE and 38 million in 230 BCE, across all the Zhou-era states.

urbanisation.value: Walled cities multiplied in the Warring States period. Capitals such as Linzi (Qi) became large commercial centres.
urbanisation.source: Li Feng, Early China: A Social and Cultural History (2013)

disease.value: No major epidemics are documented in the sources checked.

migration.value: In 771 BCE the court moved east to Wangcheng (near Luoyang) after the Quanrong sacked the western capital.

economicBase.value: Agriculture by rural households, who owed labour, taxes and military service. Dependent labourers and slaves were a minority.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade between the states grew in the Eastern Zhou, along with markets and merchant fortunes.
tradeRoutes.source: Li Feng, Early China: A Social and Cultural History (2013)

moneyAndTax.value: Bronze spade-shaped coins (“spade money”) and other coin shapes in different states. The “well-field” land system described in later texts is probably an idealised model.

inequality.value: A hereditary aristocracy held fiefs, while commoners farmed and served. Merchant wealth rose in the late period.

governmentType.value: A monarchy with a feudal (fengjian) system. The king granted hereditary fiefs to relatives and allies, ranked duke, marquis, count, viscount and baron.

keyRulers.value: King Wu (c. 1046–1043 BCE, conqueror of the Shang). The Duke of Zhou (regent). King You (781–771 BCE, killed when the capital fell). King Ping (770–720 BCE, moved east). King Nan (314–256 BCE, last).

succession.value: Patrilineal primogeniture (eldest son inherits), with kin lineages organised in a ritual hierarchy.

institutions.value: The Mandate of Heaven: rulers govern only while Heaven approves, and a ruler who misgoverns can be replaced. The Zhou used it to justify overthrowing the Shang. A court ritual system (li) and royal calendar.
institutions.source: Wikipedia: Mandate of Heaven (checked 5 Nov 2026); video research: RESEARCH.md, “5,000 Years of China”

stability.value: The Gonghe Regency (841–828 BCE) after a revolt. Royal power faded after 771 BCE. In the Warring States period (c. 475–221 BCE) the major states fought for supremacy.

eliteConflict.value: Client states grew independent. In 403 BCE the court recognised the partition of Jin into Han, Zhao and Wei, and from 344 BCE regional rulers began calling themselves kings.

armyAndTech.value: The “Six Armies of the west” and the “Eight Armies of Chengzhou”. King Wu crossed the Yellow River with a reported 45,000 men and 300 chariots. Mass infantry, crossbows and iron weapons came in the Warring States period.

majorWars.value: The conquest of the Shang (c. 1046 BCE). The Rebellion of the Three Guards. The Quanrong sack of Haojing (771 BCE). The wars of the Warring States, ending with the Qin conquest.

territoryChange.value: Western Zhou control centred on the Wei River valley and the North China Plain. Royal territory shrank to a small domain around Luoyang in the Eastern Zhou.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals included the Quanrong and southern peoples, and later the powerful states of Qin, Chu, Jin and Qi.

inventions.value: Iron casting spread in the later Zhou. There were large irrigation works such as the Sunshu Ao reservoir and Ximen Bao’s canals (5th century BCE). The crossbow was in use by the Warring States period.

scienceEducation.value: An age of thinkers: Confucius (551–479 BCE), Laozi (whose historical existence is debated), Mozi, Mencius, Xunzi and Han Fei, often called the “Hundred Schools of Thought”.
scienceEducation.source: Wikipedia: Zhou dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); video research: RESEARCH.md, “5,000 Years of China”

openness.value: The chariot (adopted under the Shang) was first used on a large scale in battle by the Zhou. Some states adopted cavalry from northern peoples in the 4th century BCE.

communicationTransport.value: Chariots for war, roads between states, canals in the late period; written orders on bamboo strips.

religion.value: Ancestor veneration, Heaven worship (Tian) and folk religion. Confucianism, Taoism and Legalism emerged as major schools of thought.

languageWriting.value: Old Chinese. Bronze-inscription script developed into seal script, and an early form of clerical script appeared by the dynasty’s end.

artsArchitecture.value: Often considered the high point of Chinese bronzeware: ritual vessels and bells. The Book of Songs (Shijing) collects poetry from this period.

socialStructure.value: King, nobles of five ranks, officials (shi), farmers, artisans and merchants. Dependent labourers and slaves were a minority.

sharedIdentity.value: A shared Zhou ritual culture (li) and the idea of a single “all under Heaven” (tianxia) under the Son of Heaven, even when politically divided.
sharedIdentity.source: Li Feng, Early China: A Social and Cultural History (2013)

dailyLife.value: Rammed-earth houses; millet, wheat, rice and soy; hemp clothing for commoners and silk for nobles.

neighbours.value: The Quanrong and other Rong and Di peoples, the southern peoples, and states such as Chu, Wu and Yue on the Yangtze.

ideasReligions.value: Zhou ideas, including the Mandate of Heaven, Confucian ethics and Taoism, became the foundation of later Chinese political thought.

colonisation.value: Expanded by settling royal kin and allies in new fiefs across the plain.

riseSignals.value: A strong base in the Wei valley, alliances against the Shang, and a powerful ideology (the Mandate of Heaven) that justified the conquest.

peakPeriod.value: The early Western Zhou (11th–10th centuries BCE), when royal power and bronze culture were strongest.

declineSignals.value: Fragmentation into rival states as royal authority faded, a key stage in the “dynastic cycle”. The 771 BCE sack of Haojing and the rise of independent kingdoms.
declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: Zhou dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); Wikipedia: Dynastic cycle (checked 5 Nov 2026)

outcome.value: Qin deposed King Nan in 256 BCE, and the last Zhou holdouts fell in 249 BCE. Qin unified China in 221 BCE.

sources.value: Bronze inscriptions, archaeology, and transmitted texts (the Book of Documents, the Spring and Autumn Annals, Zuozhuan, Shiji). Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Li Feng (2013).

overallCertainty.value: Moderate. The Western Zhou date 1046 BCE is supported by the Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project, though other dates from 1122 to 1027 BCE have been proposed. Period boundaries vary by source (Spring and Autumn: c. 771/770 to 481/476 BCE).
